tasks.solution_overview:
The model is a named polynomial of time, quantity, or cost; later claims are substitutions, derivatives, or tabled increments.

$$h(t)=\frac{1}{500}t^{3}-\frac{9}{100}t^{2}+t$$

Evaluate $h$ and $h'$ at the named times.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

tasks.title: Rebuild a Monic Cubic from Three Given Zeros
tasks.context: A monic cubic $p$ has zeros $-2$, $0$ and $4$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The sum of the zeros equals $-2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A monic cubic with zeros $-2$, $0$ and $4$ is uniquely the product of those three linear factors.

$$p(x)=x(x+2)(x-4)$$

$$(x+2)(x-4)=x^{2}-2x-8$$

$$x(x^{2}-2x-8)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-8x$$

The expanded formula is the one on the card.

The zeros of the expanded cubic are immediate:

$$x^{3}-2x^{2}-8x=x(x^{2}-2x-8)$$

$$x^{3}-2x^{2}-8x=x(x+2)(x-4)$$

, recovering $-2$, $0$ and $4$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Substitute $x=1$ into the factored cubic rather than expanding first.

$$p(1)=(1)(1+2)(1-4)$$

$$p(1)=(1)(3)(-3)$$

$$p(1)=-9$$

The value is exactly $-9$.

The expanded writing $x^{3}-2x^{2}-8x$ at $x=1$ is $1-2-8=-9$, the same height. Both the factored product $(1)(3)(-3)$ and the collected cubic therefore agree on $-9$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The constant term is $p(0)$. One of the three zeros is already $0$, so the factor $x$ kills every leftover constant.

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-8x$$

$$p(0)=0$$

There is no standalone number at the end of the expanded cubic. The constant term is $0$.

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

Equivalently, the expanded cubic $x^{3}-2x^{2}-8x$ has no standalone number at the end: every term still carries a positive power of $x$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Add the three given zeros instead of copying a sign from Vieta without looking.

$$-2+0+4$$

$$=2$$

For a monic cubic the sum of the zeros equals minus the coefficient of $x^{2}$, and that coefficient is $-2$, so the sum is $2$. The card says $-2$, which is the coefficient itself rather than the sum.

A sign error from Vieta is the usual trap: the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $-2$, and the sum of the zeros is minus that coefficient, hence $+2$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Evenness would require $p(-x)=p(x)$ identically, which fails as soon as an odd power is present.

$$p(x)=x^{3}-2x^{2}-8x$$

$$p(-x)=-x^{3}-2x^{2}+8x$$

Already $p(1)=-9$ while

$$p(-1)=(-1)-2+8$$

$$p(-1)=5$$

, so the two sides are unequal. The cubic is not even.

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be even.

Evenness also fails at the listed zeros:

$$p(2)=2\cdot 4\cdot(-2)$$

$$p(2)=-16$$

 while $p(-2)=0$, so the two sides cannot match.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem names the polynomial, the pair, or the multiplicity pattern that every later computation refers to.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

tasks.title: Far-End Behaviour Without a Formula
tasks.context: Suppose $f(x)=a_n x^{n}+\cdots+a_0$ is a real polynomial with $n\ge 1$ and $a_n\neq 0$, but no explicit coefficients are listed. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $n$ is odd and $a_n>0$, then $p(x)\to +\infty$ as $x\to +\infty$.
If $n$ is even and $a_n>0$, then $p(x)\to -\infty$ as $x\to -\infty$.
The value $p(0)$ equals the constant term $a_0$.
If $n$ is odd, then $p$ must be an odd function.
The highest power of $x$ in $p$ is $x^{n}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The cards call the stem polynomial $p$. An odd highest power with a positive lead keeps the sign of $x$ itself for large positive $x$.

$$p(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots+a_{0}$$

Factor out the highest power, using that $n$ is odd and $a_{n}>0$:

$$
p(x)=x^{n}\left(a_{n}+\frac{a_{n-1}}{x}+\cdots+\frac{a_{0}}{x^{n}}\right)
$$

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

Oddness requires the expanded formula to flip under $x\mapsto -x$.

$$p(-x)=-p(x)$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The bracket tends to $a_{n}>0$ and $x^{n}\to+\infty$, so $p(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

An even power stays positive at both ends. With $a_{n}>0$ the far-left end therefore rises, not falls.

$$p(x)=x^{2}\qquad(n$$

$$p(x)=2,\ a_{n}$$

$$p(x)=1)$$

$$\lim_{x\to-\infty}p(x)=+\infty$$

Evenness requires the expanded formula to survive $x\mapsto -x$.

$$p(-x)=p(x)$$

The same holds for any even $n$ and positive lead: $x^{n}\to+\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$, so $p(x)\to+\infty$, not to $-\infty$. The claimed dive is wrong.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Putting $x=0$ into a polynomial kills every term that still carries a positive power of $x$, and the leftover is the constant term.

$$p(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots+a_{1}x+a_{0}$$

$$p(0)=a_{0}$$

That identity is the definition of $a_{0}$, independent of $n$ and of the other coefficients.

For the running example $p(x)=x^{3}-4x+7$ one has $p(0)=7$, which is exactly the leftover constant written at the end of the formula.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Odd degree controls the two ends; oddness is the stronger identity $p(-x)=-p(x)$. A single extra even power already breaks it.

$$p(x)=x^{3}+1$$

$$p(-x)=-x^{3}+1\neq -p(x)$$

Here $n=3$ is odd, yet $p$ is not an odd function. The implication from odd degree to oddness fails.

Odd degree only forces opposite end behaviour. The extra constant $1$ in $x^{3}+1$ is an even-degree contaminant that wrecks $p(-x)=-p(x)$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The stem writes $p$ (called $f$ in the opening line) with leading term $a_{n}x^{n}$ and $a_{n}\neq 0$, so the highest surviving power is exactly $x^{n}$.

$$p(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots+a_{0},\qquad a_{n}\neq 0$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

No higher power is present, and the coefficient of $x^{n}$ is nonzero, so that power is genuinely on top. The highest power is $x^{n}$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general polynomial, so the reasoning runs on highest powers, parity, and the factor theorem instead of on a single numerical example.

Far-out behaviour is controlled by $n$ and the sign of $a_n$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

tasks.title: Workshop Output Cost and a Recorded Total Table
tasks.context: Total daily cost in euros is $C(q)=\frac{1}{50}q^{3}-\frac{3}{5}q^{2}+4q+10$ for output $q$ in units. A second line records totals in the table. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The second line's average cost per unit over $0$ to $20$ is $12$ €.
The highest interval average on the table is on $[10,15]$.
The highest power of $q$ in $C$ is $q^{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The constant term of the cost polynomial is the cost of producing nothing. Substitute $q=0$ into the given rule.

$$C(q)=\frac{1}{50}q^{3}-\frac{3}{5}q^{2}+4q+10$$

$$C(0)=10$$

The table's first column records the same $10$ €. Both readings agree with the card.

Every other term of $C$ has a positive power of $q$ and vanishes at the origin, so the workshop's idle cost is the written $+10$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Keep the cubic rule, not a round number. Substitute $q=10$.

$$C(10)=\frac{1000}{50}-\frac{3}{5}\cdot 100+40+10$$

$$C(10)=20-60+40+10$$

$$20-60+40+10$$

$$C(10)=10$$

The cost is $10$ €, not $100$ €. (The table's second line lists $90$ at $q=10$, which is a different recording and is still not $100$.) The value $100$ is wrong.

A misread $\frac{1}{50}\cdot 10^{3}=200$ would already be too large; the genuine arithmetic is $20-60+40+10=10$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The second line is the recorded totals $10,45,90,155,250$. The average cost per unit from $q=0$ to $q=20$ is the whole-run rise divided by $20$.

$$250-10$$

$$=240$$

$$\frac{240}{20}$$

$$=12$$

That average is $12$ € per unit.

In euros per unit that is $\frac{250-10}{20}=12$. The polynomial itself is a different recording and is not what the card asked for.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Interval averages on the table are first differences of the totals, each over a block of $5$ units.

$$C(q)=\frac{q^{3}}{50} - \frac{3 q^{2}}{5} + 4 q + 10$$

$$\frac{35}{5}$$

$$C(q)=7,\quad \frac{45}{5}$$

$$\frac{35}{5}$$

$$C(q)=9,\quad \frac{65}{5}$$

$$\frac{35}{5}$$

$$C(q)=13,\quad \frac{95}{5}$$

$$\frac{35}{5}$$

$$C(q)=19$$

The four averages are $7,9,13,19$ on $[0,5]$, $[5,10]$, $[10,15]$, $[15,20]$. The peak is $19$ on $[15,20]$, not $13$ on $[10,15]$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The highest power is the largest exponent whose coefficient is nonzero. The given rule opens with a cubic term.

$$C(q)=\frac{q^{3}}{50} - \frac{3 q^{2}}{5} + 4 q + 10$$

$$C(q)=\frac{1}{50}q^{3}-\frac{3}{5}q^{2}+4q+10$$

The coefficient $\frac{1}{50}$ is not zero, and no $q^{4}$ appears. The top power is $q^{3}$.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

Expanding is unnecessary: the written rule already begins with $\frac{1}{50}q^{3}$. No $q^{4}$ term is present to steal the top place.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The model is a named polynomial of time, quantity, or cost; later claims are substitutions, derivatives, or tabled increments.

$$C(q)=\frac{q^{3}}{50} - \frac{3 q^{2}}{5} + 4 q + 10$$

Interval average costs are $\Delta C/\Delta q$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

On equally spaced samples, a frozen difference layer diagnoses the degree.

tasks.title: Touching the Axis at Two, Crossing at Negative One
tasks.context: The figure shows a monic cubic that touches the $x$-axis at $x=2$ and crosses at $x=-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $p$ has exactly two distinct real zeros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A touch at $x=2$ spends an even exponent on $(x-2)$; a crossing at $x=-1$ spends an odd exponent on $(x+1)$. Degree three and a monic lead leave only one possibility.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$(x^{2}-4x+4)(x+1)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

The reconstruction is the stated product.

Near $x=2$ the squared factor does not change sign, so the graph touches and turns back; near $x=-1$ a single factor changes sign and the graph crosses.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The $y$-intercept is $p(0)$, which in factored form is the product of the constant pieces.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$p(0)=(-2)^{2}(1)$$

$$(-2)^{2}(1)$$

$$p(0)=4$$

The expanded cubic $x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$ has the same constant term $4$.

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The expanded cubic $x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$ opens with no $x$ term and ends with $+4$, confirming $p(0)=4$ a second time.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A double root is automatically a stationary point. Differentiate the reconstruction and evaluate at the touch.

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-6x$$

$$3x^{2}-6x=3x(x-2)$$

$$p'(2)=0$$

The factor $(x-2)$ in $p'$ is inherited from the squared factor in $p$, so the tangent at $x=2$ is horizontal.

The other root of $p'$ is $x=0$, a stationary point that is not on the axis, since $p(0)=4\neq 0$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Distinct zeros are the distinct numbers at which $p$ vanishes, ignoring how often each factor is repeated.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

The zero set is $\{2,-1\}$. Multiplicity accounts for three roots in total, but only two of those roots are different numbers. Exactly two distinct real zeros appear.

A multiplicity total of three is what made the cubic; it does not manufacture a third distinct abscissa. The figure shows a touch and a cross, two axis points.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The cubic is monic, so the far-right end rises.

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}\left(1-\frac{3}{x}+\frac{4}{x^{3}}\right)$$

As $x\to+\infty$ the bracket tends to $1$ and $x^{3}\to+\infty$, so $p(x)\to+\infty$, not to $-\infty$. The claimed dive contradicts the positive lead.

A leading coefficient of $-1$ would dive on the right, but this reconstruction is monic. The far-right end of the figure must rise.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

tasks.title: Graph Clues: Three Crossings and a Turn Between the Last Pair
tasks.context: The figure shows a monic cubic with $x$-intercepts $-1$, $2$ and $4$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The local minimum between $2$ and $4$ is negative.
The sum of the zeros is $5$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The $y$-intercept of a monic cubic with $x$-intercepts $-1$, $2$ and $4$ is the product of those three numbers with a sign.

$$p(x)=(x+1)(x-2)(x-4)$$

$$p(0)=(1)(-2)(-4)$$

$$(1)(-2)(-4)$$

$$p(0)=8$$

The expanded form $x^{3}-5x^{2}+2x+8$ has the same constant term $8$.

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

For a monic cubic the constant term equals $(-1)^{3}$ times the product of the zeros: $-(-1)(2)(4)=8$, matching $p(0)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Between the consecutive zeros $2$ and $4$ a monic cubic dips below the axis. Already the midpoint is negative:

$$p(3)=(4)(1)(-1)$$

$$(4)(1)(-1)$$

$$p(3)=-4$$

The stationary point in $(2,4)$ is a local minimum, and a local minimum sitting below $p(3)=-4$ is certainly negative. The local minimum between $2$ and $4$ is negative.

The graph of a monic cubic is negative throughout the last gap $(2,4)$ because only the factor $(x-4)$ is negative there. A local minimum in a negative gap is negative.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Rolle's theorem places a root of $p'$ in every gap between consecutive zeros, including the gap $(2,4)$.

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-10x+2$$

$$x=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{19}}{3}$$

The larger root is about $3.12$, which lies in $(2,4)$. So $p'(x)=0$ has a solution in that interval.

The smaller critical abscissa $\frac{5-\sqrt{19}}{3}\approx 0.21$ lies in $(-1,2)$, so each consecutive gap holds exactly one turn.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Evenness would require $p(-x)=p(x)$. A cubic with three zeros not symmetric about the origin cannot be even.

$$p(x)=x^{3}-5x^{2}+2x+8$$

$$p(1)=(2)(-1)(-3)$$

$$p(1)=6$$

$$p(-1)=(0)(-3)(-5)$$

$$p(-1)=0$$

Those two values already differ, so $p$ is not even.

An even polynomial is symmetric about the $y$-axis, but the intercepts $-1$, $2$ and $4$ are not a symmetric set, so evenness is impossible.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Add the three marked intercepts.

$$-1+2+4$$

$$=5$$

For a monic cubic that sum equals minus the coefficient of $x^{2}$. Expanding gives $x^{3}-5x^{2}+\cdots$, and $-(-5)=5$, matching. The sum of the zeros is $5$.

The same $5$ is minus the $x^{2}$ coefficient in $x^{3}-5x^{2}+2x+8$. Both Vieta and the raw sum of intercepts agree.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$p(x)=(x+1)(x-2)(x-4)$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

tasks.title: Degree of a Sum When $n>m$ (Set 1)
tasks.context: Set 1. Let $p$ have highest power $x^{n}$ and $q$ have highest power $x^{m}$, with $n>m\ge 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is $x^{n}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p\cdot q$ is $x^{n+m}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is $x^{n+m}$.
If $a_n$ and $b_m$ are both positive, $p+q$ has positive leading coefficient.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

When the highest powers are unequal, the taller one has nothing of the same degree to cancel against. Write $p=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots$ and $q=b_{m}x^{m}+\cdots$ with $n>m$ and $a_{n}\neq 0$.

$$p+q=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

The term $a_{n}x^{n}$ survives, and no higher power is present. The highest power in the sum is $x^{n}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Leading terms multiply, and the exponents add. With $a_{n}\neq 0$ and $b_{m}\neq 0$ the product of the leads cannot vanish.

$$p\cdot q=a_{n}b_{m}x^{n+m}+\cdots$$

No cancellation of the top term is possible, so the highest power in the product is $x^{n+m}$.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A concrete pair $p(x)=x^{3}$ and $q(x)=x^{2}$ produces $p\cdot q=x^{5}$ with $n+m=5$, and the coefficient $1\cdot 1$ cannot cancel.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Adding polynomials never adds the exponents; that is the product rule. A concrete pair with $n=3$ and $m=1$ separates the two operations.

$$p(x)=x^{3}$$

$$q(x)=x$$

$$p+q=x^{3}+x$$

The highest power in the sum is $x^{3}=x^{n}$, not $x^{4}=x^{n+m}$. The claimed exponent $n+m$ belongs to $p\cdot q$.

The same pair gives

$$p+q=x^{3}+x$$

, whose top power is still $x^{3}$. The exponent $n+m$ never appears in a sum.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The leading coefficient of $p+q$ is the leading coefficient of $p$, because $q$ has no $x^{n}$ term to mix with it.

$$p+q=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots$$

If $a_{n}>0$, that surviving lead is positive (the sign of $b_{m}$ is irrelevant). So $p+q$ has a positive leading coefficient.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The hypothesis also names $b_{m}>0$, but that lower-degree lead sits below $x^{n}$ and cannot flip the sign of $a_{n}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Subtracting $q$ still cannot touch the $x^{n}$ term of $p$, because $q$ has no such term.

$$p-q=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots$$

The coefficient $a_{n}$ is unchanged and nonzero, so the highest power of $p-q$ remains $x^{n}$ for every such pair.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

Taking $p(x)=x^{3}+1$ and $q(x)=x$ gives

$$p-q=x^{3}-x+1$$

, still of highest power $x^{3}$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general polynomial, so the reasoning runs on highest powers, parity, and the factor theorem instead of on a single numerical example.

Unequal top powers cannot cancel in a sum.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

No coefficients are fixed, so the reasoning runs on the structure of a general polynomial instead of on a single numerical example.

tasks.title: When Equal Leading Terms Cancel in a Sum (Set 1)
tasks.context: Exam set 1. Let $p$ and $q$ both have highest power $x^n$ with leading coefficients $a$ and $b$ satisfying $a+b=0$ and $a\neq 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is strictly less than $n$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p-q$ is still $x^{n}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p\cdot q$ is $x^{2n}$.
$p$ and $-q$ share the same leading coefficient.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Opposite leading coefficients cancel the top power of the sum. With $a+b=0$ and $a\neq 0$,

$$p+q=(a+b)x^{n}+\cdots$$

$$(a+b)x^{n}+\cdots=0\cdot x^{n}+\cdots$$

Whatever remains has strictly smaller degree (or is the zero polynomial, whose degree is not $n$ either). The highest power in $p+q$ is strictly less than $n$.

If the lower terms also happen to cancel, $p+q$ may be the zero polynomial, whose degree is still not $n$. In every case the top power drops.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Subtraction doubles the leading coefficient instead of cancelling it, because $b=-a$.

$$a-b=a-(-a)$$

$$a-(-a)=2a$$

$$p-q=2ax^{n}+\cdots$$

Since $a\neq 0$, the coefficient $2a$ is nonzero, so the highest power of $p-q$ is still $x^{n}$.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

With $p(x)=x^{2}+1$ and $q(x)=-x^{2}+x$ one gets $p-q=2x^{2}-x+1$, visibly still of highest power $x^{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Cancelling the top power does not force every lower term to vanish. A concrete pair with $a=1$ and $b=-1$ keeps a linear remainder.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+1$$

$$q(x)=-x^{2}+x$$

$$p+q=x+1$$

That sum is not the zero polynomial. Only the $x^{n}$ terms were required to cancel.

The stem only assumed $a+b=0$. It said nothing about the constant terms or the middle coefficients, which are free to survive.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The product of the two nonzero leads is nonzero, even though those leads are opposites.

$$ab=a(-a)$$

$$a(-a)=-a^{2}\neq 0$$

$$p\cdot q=-a^{2}x^{2n}+\cdots$$

The highest power is $x^{2n}$. Taking $p(x)=x^{2}+1$ and $q(x)=-x^{2}$ gives $-x^{4}-x^{2}$, still degree $4=2n$.

Because $a\neq 0$, the product of the leads cannot be zero. Cancellation in a product would require one of the two polynomials to have lead $0$, contradicting the stem.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The polynomial $-q$ has leading coefficient $-b$. The stem forces $b=-a$, so

$$-b=-(-a)$$

$$-(-a)=a$$

That is exactly the leading coefficient of $p$. The two polynomials $p$ and $-q$ therefore open with the same $ax^{n}$.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

Equivalently, $p-(-q)=p+q$ has dropped degree, which is exactly the statement that $p$ and $-q$ share a lead and cancel in a sum.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general polynomial, so the reasoning runs on highest powers, parity, and the factor theorem instead of on a single numerical example.

Opposite leading coefficients remove the top power in $p+q$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

tasks.title: Parameter k: How Many Real Zeros?
tasks.context: Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Factor out the obvious linear piece and read the remaining quadratic from the sign of $k$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

If $k>0$ then $x^{2}=k$ has two real solutions $\pm\sqrt{k}$, distinct from each other and from $0$. The three zeros $-\sqrt{k}$, $0$, $\sqrt{k}$ are distinct.

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

For the sample $k=4$ the zeros are $-2$, $0$ and $2$, three distinct reals, and $g_{4}(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The parameter value $k=0$ collapses the quadratic factor onto a repeated origin.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

The only real zero is $x=0$, now of multiplicity three. Distinct zeros are counted without multiplicity, so there is one, not three.

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

A root of multiplicity three is still a single distinct number. The graph of $x^{3}$ flattens at the origin but meets the axis only there.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

If $k<0$ then $x^{2}-k=x^{2}+|k|$ is always positive, so it contributes no real root.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

The only real solution of $g_{k}(x)=0$ is $x=0$. One real zero (simple) is exactly the count claimed.

For $k=-4$ one has

$$g(x)=x^{3}+4x$$

$$g(x)=x(x^{2}+4)$$

, and $x^{2}+4=0$ has no real solution. The graph crosses the axis only at the origin, a single simple root.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The leading term is $x^{3}$ for every real $k$. The parameter multiplies only the linear term.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

The coefficient of $x^{3}$ is $1$, independent of $k$. Changing $k$ moves the roots but never the lead.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

Comparing $g_{1}(x)=x^{3}-x$ with $g_{2}(x)=x^{3}-2x$, both still open with $x^{3}$. Only the linear coefficient moved.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Oddness is the identity $g_{k}(-x)=-g_{k}(x)$. Every term of the family carries an odd power of $x$.

$$g_{k}(-x)=(-x)^{3}-k(-x)$$

$$(-x)^{3}-k(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-(x^{3}-kx)$$

A double root at $x=1$ and a simple root at $x=-3$, together with a monic lead, pin the cubic down completely.

$$p(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+3)$$

$$(x^{2}-2x+1)(x+3)=x^{3}+x^{2}-5x+3$$

.

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}+2x-5$$

$$p'(1)=3+2-5$$

$$3+2-5$$

$$p'(1)=0$$

The tangent at the double root is horizontal.

A double root of $p$ is a root of $p'$ by the product rule: differentiating $(x-1)^{2}(x+3)$ leaves a factor $(x-1)$.

So the statement is True.

$$(-1)^{2}(3)$$

$$p(0)=3$$

Vieta's constant term for a monic cubic is $(-1)^{3}(1)(1)(-3)=3$, matching $p(0)$. Both routes give the same leftover $3$.

Count the double root twice: the multiplicity-weighted sum is $1+1+(-3)$.

$$1+1-3$$

tasks.context: Let $p(x)=x^{2} - 2 x + 3$ and $r(x)=p(x)^2-p(x)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $r$ is $x^{4}$.

**A.** → True

Squaring a quadratic produces a quartic, and subtracting $p$ cannot cancel the new $x^{4}$ term.

$$p(x)=x^{2}-2x+3$$

$$r(x)=p(x)^{2}-p(x)$$

$$p(x)^{2}-p(x)=(x^{2}-2x+3)^{2}-(x^{2}-2x+3)$$

The lead of $p^{2}$ is $(x^{2})^{2}=x^{4}$. So the highest power of $x$ in $r$ is $x^{4}$.

Expanding the square produces $x^{4}-4x^{3}+10x^{2}-12x+9$, and subtracting $p$ cannot cancel the new $x^{4}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Factor $r$ as a difference of the form $u^{2}-u$.

$$p(x)=x^{2} - 2 x + 3$$

$$r(x)=p(x)^{2}-p(x)$$

$$p(x)^{2}-p(x)=p(x)\bigl(p(x)-1\bigr)$$

That identity is purely algebraic and does not use the coefficients of $p$. The factorisation on the card is exactly $p(p-1)$.

Any identity $u^{2}-u=u(u-1)$ applies with $u=p(x)$. Substituting the quadratic is unnecessary for this factorisation.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Evaluate $p$ at $0$ first, then form $r(0)=p(0)(p(0)-1)$.

$$p(0)=3$$

$$r(0)=3\cdot(3-1)$$

$$3\cdot(3-1)$$

$$r(0)=6$$

Direct expansion $r(x)=x^{4}-4x^{3}+9x^{2}-10x+6$ has the same constant term $6$.

Directly,

$$r(0)=3^{2}-3$$

$$r(0)=6$$

. The two computations $p(p-1)$ and $p^{2}-p$ agree at the origin, and the expanded quartic $x^{4}-4x^{3}+9x^{2}-10x+6$ ends with that same $6$.

So the statement is True.

$$p(x)=x^{2} - 2 x + 3$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)^{2}+2\ge 2$$

Both pieces stay strictly positive for every real $x$, so $r$ never hits zero on $\mathbb{R}$. There are no real zeros.

tasks.title: Raising a Cubic: Crossings After a Vertical Shift (Set 1)

statements: The turning abscissas of $q$ depend on $c$.

tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For $c=0$ the shifted graph is $p$ itself. Factor and read the zeros.

$$q(x)=p(x)+c$$

$$x=0$$

**B.** → False

$$q'(x)=p'(x)$$

$$p'(x)=3x^{2}-3$$

$$x=\pm 1$$

Those two abscissas are independent of $c$. Adding a constant raises or lowers the graph but does not slide the peaks left or right.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The local maximum of $p$ is $p(-1)=2$ and the local minimum is $p(1)=-2$. Shifting by more than $2$ lifts the local maximum off the axis or drops the local minimum below it.

$$q(x)=x^{3}-3x+c$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Oddness is $p(-x)=-p(x)$. The given cubic has only odd powers.

$$q(x)=p(x)+c$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x$$

$$p(-x)=-x^{3}+3x$$

$$-x^{3}+3x=-p(x)$$

A numerical check:

$$p(-2)=-8+6$$

$$p(-2)=-2$$

 and

$$-p(2)=-(8-6)$$

$$-p(2)=-2$$

. The two sides match, as oddness requires, and $p(0)=0$ is the origin condition for an odd function.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Adding a nonzero constant destroys oddness, because an odd function must vanish at the origin.

$$q(x)=p(x)+c$$

$$q(0)=p(0)+c$$

$$p(0)+c=c$$

If $c\neq 0$ then $q(0)\neq 0$, so $q$ is not odd. Even a tiny shift such as $c=1$ gives

$$q(x)=x^{3}-3x+1$$

, which fails $q(-x)=-q(x)$. The universal claim is false.

Oddness of $p$ is not inherited by $p+c$ unless $c=0$. Letter D established oddness only for the unshifted cubic.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$$q(x)=p(x)+c$$

Vertical shifts change intercepts and root count but not turning abscissas.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

tasks.title: Degree of a Sum When $n>m$ (Set 2)
tasks.context: Set 2. Let $p$ have highest power $x^{n}$ and $q$ have highest power $x^{m}$, with $n>m\ge 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is $x^{n}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p\cdot q$ is $x^{n+m}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is $x^{n+m}$.
If $a_n$ and $b_m$ are both positive, $p+q$ has positive leading coefficient.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Unequal top powers cannot cancel in a sum. With $n>m$ the $x^{n}$ term of $p$ has no partner in $q$.

$$p+q=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots$$

The coefficient $a_{n}$ is nonzero and no higher power appears, so the highest power in $p+q$ is $x^{n}$.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A working pair: $p(x)=x^{4}$ and $q(x)=x$ give

$$p+q=x^{4}+x$$

, whose highest power is $x^{4}=x^{n}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Leading terms multiply and exponents add. Neither lead is zero, so the top term of the product survives.

$$p\cdot q=a_{n}b_{m}x^{n+m}+\cdots$$

A concrete check: $x^{3}\cdot x^{2}=x^{5}$ with $n+m=5$. The highest power in the product is $x^{n+m}$.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The coefficient $a_{n}b_{m}$ is a product of two nonzero numbers, hence nonzero. No cancellation of $x^{n+m}$ can occur.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The exponent $n+m$ is the product rule, not the sum rule. Take $n=2$ and $m=1$.

$$p(x)=x^{2}$$

$$q(x)=x$$

$$p+q=x^{2}+x$$

The highest power in the sum is $x^{2}=x^{n}$, not $x^{3}=x^{n+m}$. Adding never adds the exponents.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The same pair has product $x^{3}$, which is $x^{n+m}$, a different polynomial from the sum. Mixing the two rules is the error.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The leading coefficient of the sum is $a_{n}$, because $q$ contributes nothing at degree $n$.

$$p+q=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots$$

If $a_{n}>0$ that surviving lead is positive, whatever the sign of $b_{m}$. So $p+q$ has a positive leading coefficient.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A numerical pair $p(x)=2x^{3}$ and $q(x)=5x$ has $a_{n}=2>0$ and $b_{m}=5>0$, and $p+q=2x^{3}+5x$ still opens with $+2$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Subtracting a strictly lower-degree polynomial leaves the top term of $p$ untouched.

$$p-q=a_{n}x^{n}+\cdots$$

Since $a_{n}\neq 0$, the highest power of $p-q$ is always $x^{n}$ under the hypothesis $n>m$.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

With $p(x)=x^{3}-1$ and $q(x)=x^{2}$ one gets $p-q=x^{3}-x^{2}-1$, still of highest power $x^{3}$. The $x^{n}$ coefficient of $p$ is never touched by a strictly lower-degree $q$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general polynomial, so the reasoning runs on highest powers, parity, and the factor theorem instead of on a single numerical example.

Unequal top powers cannot cancel in a sum.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

No coefficients are fixed, so the reasoning runs on the structure of a general polynomial instead of on a single numerical example.

tasks.title: Parameter m: How Many Real Zeros?
tasks.context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 74.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Factor the family and split according to the sign of $k$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

When $k>0$ the quadratic $x^{2}-k$ has two real roots $\pm\sqrt{k}$, distinct from $0$. The three zeros $-\sqrt{k}$, $0$, $\sqrt{k}$ are distinct.

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

For $k=9$ the zeros are $-3$, $0$ and $3$. Three distinct crossings appear on the graph of $x^{3}-9x$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Setting $k=0$ removes the linear term and leaves a pure cube.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

The equation $x^{3}=0$ has the single real solution $x=0$, of multiplicity three. Distinct real zeros number one, not three.

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

The graph of $x^{3}$ meets the axis only at the origin. Multiplicity three is not three distinct zeros.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A negative parameter makes $x^{2}-k$ a sum of squares, hence always positive.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$k<0$$

$$x^{2}-k=x^{2}+|k|>0$$

Then $g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$ vanishes only at $x=0$. Exactly one real zero remains.

Example: $k=-1$ gives

$$g(x)=x^{3}+x$$

$$g(x)=x(x^{2}+1)$$

, whose only real root is $x=0$. The quadratic $x^{2}+1$ stays at least $1$ for every real $x$, so it never supplies a second crossing.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The parameter $k$ multiplies $x$, never $x^{3}$. The leading coefficient is identically $1$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

Whether $k=4$ or $k=-7$, the cubic still opens with $x^{3}$. The lead does not depend on $k$.

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The linear coefficient $-k$ depends on $k$, but that is not the lead. The lead sits on $x^{3}$ and stays $1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Check the oddness identity with the parameter still in place.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-(x^{3}-kx)$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-g_{k}(x)$$

Every term has odd degree, so the identity holds for every real $k$, including $k=0$. The family is odd for every real $k$.

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be odd.

The identity does not use the value of $k$ at all: every surviving power of $x$ is odd, which is the whole oddness test.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

tasks.title: Downward Cubic Through the Origin
tasks.context: The figure shows a cubic with leading coefficient $-1$ and zeros $0$, $2$ and $5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product of the zeros equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Far out on the right a cubic is dominated by its leading term, and the figure fixes that term as $-x^{3}$.

$$p(x)=-x(x-2)(x-5)$$

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+7x^{2}-10x$$

Dividing through by $x^{3}$ leaves $-1+\frac{7}{x}-\frac{10}{x^{2}}$, which tends to $-1$, so for large positive $x$ the sign of $p$ matches the sign of $-x^{3}$.

$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}p(x)=-\infty$$

An odd highest power with a negative coefficient therefore falls on the far right.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A listed zero is an input where the graph meets the axis, which here means a linear factor vanishes.

$$p(x)=-x(x-2)(x-5)$$

$$p(2)=-2\cdot 0\cdot(-3)$$

$$p(2)=0$$

The middle factor is zero, so the whole product is zero independently of the remaining factors and of the leading $-1$. The expanded check $-8+28-20=0$ gives the same height. The graph crosses at $x=2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Three distinct axis crossings force a turn in each open interval between them.

$$p'(x)=-3x^{2}+14x-10$$

$$14^{2}-4\cdot 3\cdot 10$$

$$p'(x)=76$$

The discriminant is positive, so the quadratic $p'$ has two distinct real roots, and a cubic cannot have more than two. Rolle's theorem already places one stationary point in $(0,2)$ and one in $(2,5)$. Two turning points occur.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The height at the origin is the constant term, and one of the three zeros is $0$ itself.

$$p(x)=-x(x-2)(x-5)$$

$$p(0)=0$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

A strict inequality $p(0)>0$ would need a positive intercept. Expanding gives

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+7x^{2}-10x$$

, whose constant term is $0$, so the graph passes through the origin rather than sitting above it. The value $0$ is not greater than $0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The three zeros marked on the figure are $0$, $2$ and $5$; the product of a list that contains $0$ is $0$.

$$0\cdot 2\cdot 5$$

$$=0$$

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+7x^{2}-10x$$

Vieta agrees: for $p(x)=-x^{3}+\cdots$ the constant term is $0$, which is $(-1)^{3}$ times the leading coefficient times the product of the zeros. The product is $0$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$p(x)=-x \left(x^{2} - 7 x + 10\right)$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

tasks.title: Odd Cubic Against a Parabola
tasks.context: Let $p(x)=x^{3} - x$ and $\ell(x)=x^{2} - 1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graphs meet at least twice on the real line.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Meetings are the real roots of the difference $p-\ell$, so subtract the two rules and factor.

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{3}-x-(x^{2}-1)$$

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{3}-x^{2}-x+1$$

$$(x-1)^{2}(x+1)=0$$

The roots are $x=1$ (a double meeting) and $x=-1$ (a simple crossing). Checking the original pair:

$$p(1)=0$$

$$p(1)=\ell(1)$$

 and

$$p(-1)=-(-1)-1$$

$$p(-1)=0$$

$$p(-1)=\ell(-1)$$

. That is already two distinct real abscissas.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The highest power of a difference is the highest power that does not cancel, and here the two leading terms are $x^{3}$ and $x^{2}$.

$$p(x)=x^{3} - x$$

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{3}-x^{2}-x+1$$

The cubic term survives because $\ell$ has no $x^{3}$ to cancel it, while every lower power is allowed to remain.

$$x^{3}$$

A polynomial whose top surviving power is $x^{3}$ is cubic.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Evenness is the identity $p(-x)=p(x)$ on the whole line, so substitute $-x$ and compare.

$$p(x)=x^{3} - x$$

$$p(-x)=(-x)^{3}-(-x)$$

$$p(-x)=-x^{3}+x$$

$$p(-x)=-(x^{3}-x)$$

$$-(x^{3}-x)=-p(x)$$

The two sides are opposites, which is the odd test, not the even one. A numerical check:

$$p(2)=8-2$$

$$p(2)=6$$

 while $p(-2)=-8+2=-6\neq 6$. Only odd powers appear in $x^{3}-x$, so $p$ is odd rather than even.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

A linear function has highest power $x^{1}$, so read the written rule for $\ell$ by descending powers.

$$\ell(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The top term is $x^{2}$, with leading coefficient $1$, and there is no linear term at all.

$$x^{2}$$

Evaluating at two points shows the bend: $\ell(0)=-1$ and $\ell(2)=3$. A line has highest power $x^{1}$, but the written top term is $x^{2}$. A polynomial whose highest power is $x^{2}$ is quadratic, not linear.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Two graphs have the same height at $x=0$ only if their constant terms agree.

$$p(0)=0^{3}-0$$

$$0^{3}-0$$

$$p(0)=0$$

$$\ell(0)=0^{2}-1$$

$$0^{2}-1$$

$$\ell(0)=-1$$

$$0=-1$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The cubic passes through the origin while the parabola sits one unit below it. Even a nearby check $p(1)=0$ against $\ell(1)=0$ is a meeting elsewhere, not at $x=0$. The two values at $0$ are different.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem names the polynomial that every later computation refers to.

$$p(x)=x^{3} - x$$

$$p(x)=x^{3} - x$$

Meetings solve $p-\ell=0$, i.e. $x^{3} - x^{2} - x + 1=0$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

tasks.title: R: Stall Revenue Model
tasks.context: A model gives $R(n)=\frac{n \left(- n^{2} + 60 n + 200\right)}{20}$ for $n\ge 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $n$ in $R$ is $n^{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Revenue increases at a named input when the derivative is positive there, so expand $R$ and differentiate.

$$R(n)=\frac{-n^{3}+60n^{2}+200n}{20}$$

$$R'(n)=\frac{-3n^{2}+120n+200}{20}$$

$$R'(8)=\frac{-192+960+200}{20}$$

$$R'(8)=\frac{242}{5}$$

The value $\frac{242}{5}$ is positive, so the model is still climbing at $n=8$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Substitute $n=8$ into the factored model rather than estimating from a sketch.

$$R(8)=\frac{8\bigl(-64+480+200\bigr)}{20}$$

$$R(8)=\frac{8\cdot 616}{20}$$

$$R(8)=\frac{4928}{20}$$

$$R(8)=\frac{1232}{5}$$

Cancel a factor of $4$ in the fraction: $4928\div 4=1232$ and $20\div 4=5$, so the value is $\frac{1232}{5}$. The exact value is the quoted fraction.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The highest power is the largest exponent whose coefficient survives after the constant $20$ is distributed.

$$R(n)=-\frac{1}{20}n^{3}+3n^{2}+10n$$

The $n^{3}$ term has coefficient $-\frac{1}{20}\neq 0$, so it is not cancelled by anything in the numerator.

$$n^{3}$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

No higher power appears, and the cubic term is present.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The constant term of a polynomial is its value at $0$, and this model has an explicit factor of $n$.

$$R(n)=\frac{n(-n^{2}+60n+200)}{20}$$

$$R(0)=\frac{0\cdot 200}{20}$$

$$R(0)=0$$

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

With no sales the predicted revenue is zero. Expanding gives

$$R(n)=-\frac{1}{20}n^{3}+3n^{2}+10n$$

, which has no constant term, so $R(0)=0$ identically. The value is $0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A quadratic function has highest power $n^{2}$ and nothing above it, so look at the expanded rule.

$$R(n)=-\frac{1}{20}n^{3}+3n^{2}+10n$$

The cubic term is present with a nonzero coefficient, so the graph is not a parabola.

$$-\frac{1}{20}n^{3}$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A model whose top power is $n^{3}$ is cubic rather than quadratic.

So the statement is False.

Differentiate $R$ and evaluate at the named input.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

tasks.title: Finite Differences Diagnose the Degree (Set 2)
tasks.context: Sample set 2: a polynomial $p$ is tabulated below. Evaluate each statements. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Read the column whose argument is $x=1$ directly from the table, then confirm against the proposed closed form.

$$p(1)=4$$

The same number comes from substituting into $3x^{2}-x+2$.

$$3\cdot 1^{2}-1+2$$

$$p(1)=4$$

The neighbouring columns agree as well: $p(0)=2$ and $p(2)=12$ sit on either side of this height $4$. Both routes give $4$, matching the listed height.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

On unit spacing a linear source would make the first differences a constant row, so subtract consecutive outputs.

$$4-2$$

$$=2,\quad 12-4$$

$$4-2$$

$$=8,\quad 26-12$$

$$4-2$$

$$=14$$

$$46-26$$

$$=20,\quad 72-46$$

$$20,\quad 72-46$$

$$=26$$

If a lower difference layer still moves, the degree is strictly higher than that layer's index.

Those jumps $2,8,14,20,26$ grow by $6$ each time; a constant first-difference row would be required for a line. The first differences are not constant.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The last tabulated argument is $x=5$, and the last listed height is $72$.

$$p(5)=72$$

The closed form $3x^{2}-x+2$ reproduces that column independently.

$$3\cdot 25-5+2$$

$$p(5)=72$$

A neighbouring check $p(4)=46$ from both the table and $3\cdot 16-4+2$ sits next to this last column. The table and the algebraic rule agree on $72$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Check the proposed quadratic against every tabulated column rather than against a single point.

$$3\cdot 0^{2}-0+2$$

$$=2$$

$$3\cdot 4^{2}-4+2$$

$$=46$$

$$3\cdot 25-5+2$$

$$=72$$

The remaining columns $x=1,2,3$ likewise return $4$, $12$ and $26$. Second differences of the table are constantly $6$, matching $2!\cdot 3$ for this leading coefficient. Every listed height matches $3x^{2}-x+2$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A linear model needs constant first differences, but the second differences of this table have already settled.

$$8-2$$

$$=6,\quad 14-8$$

$$8-2$$

$$=6,\quad 20-14$$

$$8-2$$

$$=6,\quad 26-20$$

$$8-2$$

$$=6$$

Constant second differences of $6$ are the signature of a quadratic with leading coefficient $3$, since $2\cdot 3=6$ on unit spacing.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}-x+2$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The samples come from a parabola, not from a line.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Rebuild from a Double Root and a Simple Root (Set 2)
tasks.context: Level 4/5, set 2. A monic cubic $p$ has a double root at $x=2$ and a simple root at $x=-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The multiplicity-weighted sum of roots is $3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A monic cubic is uniquely fixed by its roots with multiplicity: a square at $2$ and a simple factor at $-1$.

$$p(x)=(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$$

$$(x^{2}-4x+4)(x+1)=x^{3}+x^{2}-4x^{2}-4x+4x+4$$

$$p(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$$

Any other cubic with this root pattern would be a constant multiple, and monic normalisation forces that constant to be $1$. The reconstruction is the stated product.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A root of multiplicity at least two is always a root of the derivative, so differentiate the product.

$$p'(x)=2(x-2)(x+1)+(x-2)^{2}$$

$$p'(x)=(x-2)\bigl(2x+2+x-2\bigr)$$

$$(x-2)\bigl(2x+2+x-2\bigr)=(x-2)\cdot 3x$$

$$p'(2)=0$$

The factor $(x-2)$ remains in $p'$, so the tangent at the double root is horizontal. Expanding $p'(x)=3x^{2}-6x$ and substituting $x=2$ likewise gives

$$12-12$$

$$p'(2)=0$$

. The derivative vanishes at $x=2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A simple root has no reason to be stationary: the leftover factor of $p'$ need not vanish there.

$$p'(x)=3x(x-2)$$

$$p'(-1)=3(-1)(-3)$$

$$3(-1)(-3)$$

$$p'(-1)=9$$

The horizontal tangents sit at $x=0$ and at the double root $x=2$, not at $x=-1$. Expanding $p'(x)=3x^{2}-6x$ gives

$$p'(-1)=3+6$$

$$p'(-1)=9$$

 by the same arithmetic. The slope at the simple zero is $9$, not $0$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The constant term is the height at $x=0$, which can be read from the factors without expanding.

$$p(0)=(-2)^{2}(1)$$

$$(-2)^{2}(1)$$

$$p(0)=4$$

The factor test is the substitution that asks whether the height vanishes at that abscissa.

The expanded form $x^{3}-3x^{2}+4$ displays the same constant $4$, and Vieta agrees: $(-1)^{3}\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot(-1)=4$. A nearby value

$$p(1)=(1-2)^{2}(2)$$

$$p(1)=-2$$

 is not the constant term. The constant term is $4$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Vieta counts each root as often as its multiplicity, and the double root at $2$ must be added twice.

$$2+2+(-1)$$

$$=3$$

For a monic cubic that sum equals minus the coefficient of $x^{2}$.

$$-(-3)$$

$$=3$$

For a monic polynomial Vieta reads the elementary symmetric sums from the lower coefficients.

Both routes give $3$, matching the multiplicity-weighted sum of the roots. Counting without multiplicity would give the unweighted total $2+(-1)=1$, which is the wrong tally here. The weighted sum is $3$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The stem names the polynomial, the pair, or the multiplicity pattern that every later computation refers to.

$p(x)=(x-2)^2(x+1)$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

tasks.title: Square of a Quadratic Minus Itself (Set 2)
tasks.context: Let $p(x)=x^{2} + x + 1$ and $r(x)=p(x)^2-p(x)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $r$ is $x^{4}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Squaring a quadratic produces a quartic, and subtracting $p$ cannot cancel that top term.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+x+1$$

$$r(x)=(x^{2}+x+1)^{2}-(x^{2}+x+1)$$

$$r(x)=x^{4}+2x^{3}+2x^{2}+x$$

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

The leading piece of the square is $(x^{2})^{2}=x^{4}$, with coefficient $1$, and $p$ has no $x^{4}$ to cancel it. The highest power of $r$ is $x^{4}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Factor $r$ by taking out the common $p$, which is an algebraic identity rather than a special feature of this quadratic.

$$p(x)=x^{2} + x + 1$$

$$r(x)=p(x)^{2}-p(x)$$

$$r(x)=p(x)\bigl(p(x)-1\bigr)$$

Expanding the right-hand side returns $p^{2}-p$, exactly the definition in the stem.

$$p(p-1)=p^{2}-p$$

The two expressions are identical as polynomials.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The value at $0$ is the constant term of $r$, and it can be read from $p(0)$ without expanding the quartic.

$$p(0)=1$$

$$r(0)=1^{2}-1$$

$$1^{2}-1$$

$$r(0)=0$$

Equivalently,

$$r(0)=p(0)\bigl(p(0)-1\bigr)$$

$$r(0)=1\cdot 0$$

$$r(0)=0$$

. Either way the graph of $r$ meets the origin.

$$r(x)=x(x+1)(x^{2}+x+1)$$

The factor $x$ makes $r(0)=0$ visible.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A real zero of $r$ is a real zero of $p$ or of $p-1$, so inspect the two factors separately.

$$p(x)=x^{2} + x + 1$$

$$p(x)-1=x^{2}+x$$

$$x^{2}+x=x(x+1)$$

$$x(x+1)=0$$

The roots $x=0$ and $x=-1$ are real, and $p(x)=x^{2}+x+1$ itself has negative discriminant $1-4=-3$ so it never vanishes. Still, $r$ already vanishes at $0$ and at $-1$. Real zeros exist.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The leading coefficient of a square is the square of the inner lead, and here that inner lead is $1$.

$$p(x)=x^{2} + x + 1$$

$$r(x)=x^{4}+2x^{3}+2x^{2}+x$$

The coefficient of $x^{4}$ is $1$, coming from $(x^{2})^{2}$. A leading $2$ would require $p$ to start with $\sqrt{2}\,x^{2}$ or a similar rescaling, which it does not.

$$1\neq 2$$

The leading coefficient of $r$ is $1$, not $2$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:

$$p(x)=x^{2} + x + 1$$

$r=p^{2}-p=p(p-1)$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

tasks.title: Even Quartic: Factor Then Read the Shape (Set 2)
tasks.context: Let $p(x)=x^{4} - 10 x^{2} + 9$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The stem already writes $p$ in descending even powers; factoring as a quadratic in $x^{2}$ recovers the same coefficients.

$$p(x)=x^{4}-10x^{2}+9$$

$$p(x)=(x^{2}-1)(x^{2}-9)$$

$$p(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-3)(x+3)$$

Expanding the four linear factors returns $x^{4}-10x^{2}+9$ with nothing left over. The displayed rule is exactly $p$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Evenness is the identity $p(-x)=p(x)$, and a polynomial of only even powers satisfies it automatically.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 10 x^{2} + 9$$

$$p(-x)=(-x)^{4}-10(-x)^{2}+9$$

$$p(-x)=x^{4}-10x^{2}+9$$

$$p(-x)=p(x)$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be even.

Every exponent here is even, so substituting $-x$ changes nothing. A numerical check

$$p(2)=16-40+9$$

$$p(2)=-15$$

$$p(2)=p(-2)$$

 agrees. The graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The real zeros are the roots of the linear factors after the difference of squares is used twice.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 10 x^{2} + 9$$

$$p(x)=(x^{2}-1)(x^{2}-9)$$

$$x=\pm 1,\quad x$$

$$\pm 1,\quad x=\pm 3$$

Those four numbers $-3,-1,1,3$ are distinct, and each makes one factor vanish while the others stay nonzero. Direct substitution:

$$p(1)=1-10+9$$

$$p(1)=0$$

 and

$$p(3)=81-90+9$$

$$p(3)=0$$

. Four distinct real zeros occur.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Far from the origin the leading term $x^{4}$ dominates, and an even power with a positive coefficient lifts both ends.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 10 x^{2} + 9$$

$$
p(x)=x^{4}\left(1-\frac{10}{x^{2}}+\frac{9}{x^{4}}\right)
$$

The bracket tends to $1$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, so $p$ has the sign of $x^{4}$, which is positive.

$$\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}p(x)=+\infty$$

Both ends of the graph rise.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A cubic function has highest power $x^{3}$ and nothing above it, so read the written rule by descending powers.

$$p(x)=x^{4}-10x^{2}+9$$

The top term is $x^{4}$, with leading coefficient $1$.

$$x^{4}$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A polynomial whose highest power is $x^{4}$ is quartic, not cubic. There is not even an $x^{3}$ term in the expansion, so the cubic label fails twice over.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Raising a Cubic: Crossings After a Vertical Shift (Set 2)
tasks.context: The figure shows $p(x)=x^{3} - x$. Let $q(x)=p(x)+c$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The turning abscissas of $q$ depend on $c$.
There exists $c$ for which $q$ has only one real zero.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

With $c=0$ the shifted graph is $p$ itself, and $p$ factors into three distinct linear pieces.

$$q(x)=p(x)+c$$

$$q(x)=x^{3}-x$$

$$q(x)=x(x-1)(x+1)$$

The zeros are $-1$, $0$ and $1$, three different real numbers. Direct checks: $q(0)=0$, $q(1)=0$ and $q(-1)=0$. For this unshifted case $c=0$ the axis is crossed three times.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A vertical shift adds a constant, which disappears upon differentiating, so the stationary abscissas cannot move with $c$.

$$q(x)=x^{3}-x+c$$

$$q'(x)=3x^{2}-1$$

$$x=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$

Those two solutions of $q'=0$ make no reference to $c$. The turning points slide up or down as $c$ changes, but they keep the same $x$-coordinates.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A large enough vertical shift can push the local max and min onto the same side of the axis, leaving a single real root.

$$q(x)=x^{3}-x+1$$

The local values of $p$ are $\pm\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\approx\pm 0.385$, so for $c=1$ both turning heights of $q$ stay positive.

$$q(-2)=-8+2+1$$

$$-8+2+1$$

$$q(-2)=-5$$

and at the origin

$$q(0)=1$$

One sign change from $q(-2)$ to $q(0)$ and none afterwards: exactly one real zero. Such a $c$ exists.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Oddness is the identity $p(-x)=-p(x)$, and every term of $x^{3}-x$ carries an odd power.

$$q(x)=p(x)+c$$

$$p(-x)=(-x)^{3}-(-x)$$

$$p(-x)=-x^{3}+x$$

$$p(-x)=-(x^{3}-x)$$

$$-(x^{3}-x)=-p(x)$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be odd.

The identity holds on the whole line. A numerical check

$$p(2)=8-2$$

$$p(2)=6$$

 and

$$p(-2)=-8+2$$

$$p(-2)=-6$$

$$p(-2)=-p(2)$$

 agrees. Only odd powers appear in $x^{3}-x$, so $p$ is odd.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Adding a nonzero constant breaks oddness, because the constant does not change sign with $x$.

$$q(-x)=-x^{3}+x+c$$

$$-q(x)=-x^{3}+x-c$$

These agree for every $x$ only if $c=-c$, hence only if $c=0$. For the sample $c=1$ one has $q(-1)=1$ while $-q(1)=-1$. Adding $c$ is a vertical shift, which destroys the origin-symmetry of an odd graph. The shifted graph is not odd for every $c$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$$q(x)=p(x)+c$$

$$p(x)=x^{3} - x$$

Vertical shifts change intercepts and root count but not turning abscissas.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

tasks.title: Degree of a Sum When $n>m$ (Set 3)
tasks.context: Set 3. Let $p$ have highest power $x^{n}$ and $q$ have highest power $x^{m}$, with $n>m\ge 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is $x^{n}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p\cdot q$ is $x^{n+m}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is $x^{n+m}$.
If $a_n$ and $b_m$ are both positive, $p+q$ has positive leading coefficient.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

When the highest powers are unequal they cannot cancel in a sum, so the top term of $p$ survives.

$$p(x)=x^{3}$$

together with

$$q(x)=2x$$

$$p(x)+q(x)=x^{3}+2x$$

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

Here

$$n=3>m$$

$$n=1$$

, and the surviving top power is $x^{3}=x^{n}$. In general the leading term of $p$ has nothing of the same power in $q$ to cancel it. The highest power in $p+q$ is $x^{n}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Leading terms multiply and the exponents add, and the product of two nonzero leading coefficients stays nonzero.

$$p(x)=x^{3}$$

together with

$$q(x)=2x$$

$$p(x)q(x)=2x^{4}$$

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

The top power is

$$x^{4}=x^{3+1}$$

$$x^{4}=x^{n+m}$$

. The same counting holds for any $n>m$: the coefficient $a_n b_m$ cannot vanish. The highest power in the product is $x^{n+m}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Adding never adds the exponents; that arithmetic belongs to a product. A concrete pair separates the two rules.

$$p(x)+q(x)=x^{3}+2x$$

The highest power here is $x^{3}=x^{n}$, not $x^{4}=x^{n+m}$.

$$n+m=4\neq 3$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The sum keeps the larger of the two input powers, so claiming $x^{n+m}$ for $p+q$ misapplies the product rule.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The leading coefficient of $p+q$ is the leading coefficient of $p$, because $q$ has no matching power to combine with $a_n$.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+1$$

together with

$$q(x)=3x$$

$$p(x)+q(x)=x^{2}+3x+1$$

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

Both $a_2=1$ and $b_1=3$ are positive, and the lead of the sum is $1$, which is positive. In general that lead is $a_n$ itself. A positive $a_n$ therefore makes the lead of $p+q$ positive.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Subtracting $q$ still leaves the leading term of $p$ untouched, since $q$ has no $x^{n}$ term when $n>m$.

$$p(x)-q(x)=x^{3}-2x$$

The highest power remains $x^{3}=x^{n}$. The same holds for every such pair: the coefficient of $x^{n}$ in $p-q$ is $a_n\neq 0$.

$$x^{n}$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

The difference always keeps highest power $x^{n}$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general polynomial, so the reasoning runs on highest powers, parity, and the factor theorem instead of on a single numerical example.

Unequal top powers cannot cancel in a sum.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

No coefficients are fixed, so the reasoning runs on the structure of a general polynomial instead of on a single numerical example.

tasks.title: When Equal Leading Terms Cancel in a Sum (Set 2)
tasks.context: Exam set 2. Let $p$ and $q$ both have highest power $x^n$ with leading coefficients $a$ and $b$ satisfying $a+b=0$ and $a\neq 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $p+q$ is strictly less than $n$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p-q$ is still $x^{n}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $p\cdot q$ is $x^{2n}$.
$p$ and $-q$ share the same leading coefficient.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Opposite leading coefficients cancel the top power of the sum, dropping the highest remaining exponent strictly below $n$.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+1$$

together with

$$q(x)=-x^{2}+x$$

$$p(x)+q(x)=x+1$$

Here $n=2$ and

$$a+b=1+(-1)$$

$$a+b=0$$

, so the $x^{2}$ terms cancel and the sum has highest power $x^{1}$. In general the coefficient of $x^{n}$ in $p+q$ is $a+b=0$. The highest power of $p+q$ is strictly less than $n$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Subtracting reverses the sign of $b$, so the top coefficients no longer cancel: they double.

$$p(x)-q(x)=\bigl(x^{2}+1\bigr)-\bigl(-x^{2}+x\bigr)$$

$$p(x)-q(x)=2x^{2}-x+1$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

The leading coefficient is $a-b=a-(-a)=2a\neq 0$, since $a\neq 0$. In the example the top term is $2x^{2}$, so the highest power of $p-q$ remains $x^{n}$ with $n=2$. Subtracting cannot cancel opposite leads.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Cancellation of the leading terms does not force every lower coefficient to vanish, so $p+q$ need not be the zero polynomial.

$$p(x)+q(x)=x+1$$

That sum is linear, not identically zero. A second pair $x^{n}$ and $-x^{n}+1$ likewise leaves the constant $1$.

$$x^{n}+(-x^{n}+1)=1$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

Only the top power is guaranteed to disappear, so $p+q$ is not forced to be the zero polynomial.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Leading coefficients multiply, and

$$ab=a(-a)$$

$$ab=-a^{2}$$

 is nonzero because $a\neq 0$.

$$p(x)q(x)=(x^{2}+1)(-x^{2}+x)$$

$$p(x)q(x)=-x^{4}+x^{3}-x^{2}+x$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

The top power is $x^{4}=x^{2n}$. In general the product of two degree-$n$ polynomials with nonzero leads has highest power $x^{2n}$. The product keeps $x^{2n}$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The leading coefficient of $-q$ is $-b$, and the hypothesis $a+b=0$ rewrites as $-b=a$.

$$-q(x)=x^{2}-x$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

That leading coefficient is $1$, which is exactly the leading coefficient $a$ of $p(x)=x^{2}+1$. In general $-q$ starts with $-b\,x^{n}=a\,x^{n}$, the same top term as $p$. So $p$ and $-q$ share the leading coefficient $a$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general polynomial, so the reasoning runs on highest powers, parity, and the factor theorem instead of on a single numerical example.

Opposite leading coefficients remove the top power in $p+q$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

tasks.title: Parameter t: How Many Real Zeros?
tasks.context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 85.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Factor out $x$ and read the remaining quadratic: three distinct real zeros appear precisely when that quadratic has two nonzero real roots.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

Take $k=4>0$. Then $x^{2}=4$, so the zeros are $-2$, $0$ and $2$.

$$g_{4}(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

Those three numbers are distinct. The same pattern $0,\pm\sqrt{k}$ holds for every $k>0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Setting the parameter to zero collapses the family to a pure cube, which has only one distinct real zero.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}-0\cdot x$$

$$x^{3}-0\cdot x=x^{3}$$

$$x^{3}=0$$

The only real solution is $x=0$, now of multiplicity three. Three distinct zeros would need three different numbers, and a triple root at the origin is just one number. The case $k=0$ fails the count.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A negative parameter makes $x^{2}-k$ a sum of squares, hence always positive, so the factorisation leaves only the root $x=0$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

For $k=-4$ this is $x(x^{2}+4)$, and $x^{2}+4\ge 4>0$ for every real $x$.

$$x^{2}+4=0$$

has no real solution. The only real zero is $x=0$, so a negative $k$ leaves a single real zero.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The leading coefficient is the number in front of $x^{3}$, and that number is written as $1$ for every member of the family.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x^{3}-kx$$

$$g_{1}(x)=x^{3}-x$$

and

$$g_{5}(x)=x^{3}-5x$$

Both start with $x^{3}$. The parameter $k$ only rescales the linear term; it never touches the cubic coefficient. The leading coefficient is constantly $1$, independent of $k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Oddness is the identity $g_{k}(-x)=-g_{k}(x)$, and both terms of the family carry odd powers of $x$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=(-x)^{3}-k(-x)$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-(x^{3}-kx)$$

$$-(x^{3}-kx)=-g_{k}(x)$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be odd.

The parameter $k$ rides along untouched, so the identity holds for every real $k$, including $k=0$. The family is odd for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

tasks.title: Negative Leading Coefficient Cubic
tasks.context: The figure shows a cubic with leading coefficient $-1$ and zeros $-2$, $0$ and $3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product of the zeros equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The right-hand end of a cubic is settled by the leading term $-x^{3}$, which the figure names explicitly.

$$p(x)=-x(x+2)(x-3)$$

$$p(x)=-x^{3}+x^{2}+6x$$

For large positive $x$ the cubic term dominates, and $-x^{3}$ is large and negative.

$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}p(x)=-\infty$$

Odd degree with a negative lead therefore dives on the far right.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The origin is listed as a zero, which is the statement that the graph meets the axis at $x=0$.

$$p(x)=-x(x+2)(x-3)$$

$$p(0)=0\cdot(-2)\cdot(-3)$$

$$0\cdot(-2)\cdot(-3)$$

$$p(0)=0$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The explicit factor $-x$ vanishes at the origin, so the product is zero regardless of the other two roots. The expanded form $-0+0+0=0$ agrees. The intercept is $0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Three distinct real zeros place one stationary point in each gap, and a cubic cannot have more than two.

$$p'(x)=-3x^{2}+2x+6$$

$$2^{2}-4(-3)(6)$$

$$p'(x)=76$$

The discriminant is positive, so $p'$ has two distinct real roots. Rolle's theorem already puts one of them in $(-2,0)$ and the other in $(0,3)$. Two turning points occur.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A strict inequality $p(0)>0$ needs a positive intercept, but $0$ is itself a listed zero.

$$p(x)=-x(x+2)(x-3)$$

$$p(0)=0$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The graph passes through the origin rather than sitting above it. Expanding $p(x)=-x^{3}+x^{2}+6x$ shows the constant term is $0$, so the intercept is not positive. The number $0$ is not greater than $0$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The three zeros named on the figure are $-2$, $0$ and $3$, and any product that includes $0$ is $0$.

$$(-2)\cdot 0\cdot 3$$

$$=0$$

The expanded rule $p(x)=-x^{3}+x^{2}+6x$ has constant term $0$, matching that product. Vieta for a cubic $-x^{3}+\cdots$ ties the constant term to the signed product of the zeros, here $0$. The product of the zeros is $0$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The figure prints no expanded formula, so the polynomial is recovered from the ticks: zeros, intercept, and the far-field sign.

$p(x)=-x \left(x^{2} - x - 6\right)$.

A value is obtained by substituting the named number and collecting powers.

The factor theorem is a substitution: $x-r$ divides a polynomial if and only if the value at $r$ is zero.

tasks.title: Quartic Minus a Parabola
tasks.context: Let $p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$ and $\ell(x)=x^{2} - 1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graphs meet at least twice on the real line.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Meetings solve $p-\ell=0$, so subtract and factor the resulting even quartic as a quadratic in $x^{2}$.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$$

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{4}-5x^{2}+4-(x^{2}-1)$$

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}+5$$

$$(x^{2}-1)(x^{2}-5)=0$$

The real solutions are $x=\pm 1$ and $x=\pm\sqrt{5}$, four distinct meetings. That is certainly at least two.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The highest power of $p-\ell$ is the highest power that does not cancel, and both $p$ and $\ell$ are even.

$$p(x)-\ell(x)=x^{4}-6x^{2}+5$$

The $x^{4}$ term of $p$ has no counterpart in $\ell$, so it survives.

$$x^{4}$$

Evenness requires the expanded formula to survive $x\mapsto -x$.

$$p(-x)=p(x)$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A polynomial whose top power is $x^{4}$ is quartic, not cubic. The $x^{3}$ coefficient in $p-\ell$ is $0$ as well, so the cubic label has nothing to attach to.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Evenness is the identity $p(-x)=p(x)$, and every exponent in $p$ is even.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$$

$$p(-x)=(-x)^{4}-5(-x)^{2}+4$$

$$p(-x)=x^{4}-5x^{2}+4$$

$$p(-x)=p(x)$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be even.

Substituting $-x$ leaves the formula unchanged. A numerical check

$$p(2)=16-20+4$$

$$p(2)=0$$

$$p(2)=p(-2)$$

 agrees, as does

$$p(1)=1-5+4$$

$$p(1)=0$$

$$p(1)=p(-1)$$

. The graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A linear function has highest power $x^{1}$, so inspect the written rule for $\ell$.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$$

$$\ell(x)=x^{2}-1$$

The top term is $x^{2}$, with leading coefficient $1$.

$$x^{2}$$

That is a quadratic, not a line. The graph of $\ell$ is a parabola: $\ell(0)=-1$ and $\ell(2)=3$ already fail to sit on a line of slope matching a single power $x$. The highest power is $x^{2}$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Compare the two constant terms, which are the heights at $x=0$.

$$p(0)=4$$

$$\ell(0)=-1$$

$$4=-1$$

The same number is the constant term of the expanded formula.

The quartic sits four units above the origin while the parabola sits one unit below it. A meeting at $x=0$ would require $p(0)=\ell(0)$, that is $4=-1$, which is false. Those two constant terms differ exactly.

So the statement is False.

$$p(x)=x^{4} - 5 x^{2} + 4$$

Meetings solve $p-\ell=0$, i.e. $x^{4} - 6 x^{2} + 5=0$.

tasks.title: H: Tank Height
tasks.context: A model gives $H(t)=\frac{t \left(t^{2} - 50 t + 200\right)}{200}$ for $t\ge 0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $t$ in $H$ is $t^{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The model is rising at a named time only if $H'$ is positive there, so expand and differentiate.

$$H(t)=\frac{t^{3}-50t^{2}+200t}{200}$$

$$H'(t)=\frac{3t^{2}-100t+200}{200}$$

$$H'(12)=\frac{432-1200+200}{200}$$

$$H'(12)=\frac{-71}{25}$$

The value $-\frac{71}{25}$ is negative, so the tank is falling at $t=12$ rather than rising.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Substitute $t=12$ into the factored model and simplify the fraction.

$$H(12)=\frac{12\bigl(144-600+200\bigr)}{200}$$

$$H(12)=\frac{12\cdot(-256)}{200}$$

$$H(12)=\frac{-3072}{200}$$

$$H(12)=-\frac{384}{25}$$

The exact height is the quoted value. As a decimal that is $-15.36$, matching $-384\div 25$. The substitution agrees with the claim.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Distribute the constant $200$ and read the largest surviving exponent.

$$H(t)=\frac{1}{200}t^{3}-\frac{1}{4}t^{2}+t$$

The coefficient of $t^{3}$ is $\frac{1}{200}\neq 0$, so that term is present.

$$t^{3}$$

tasks.title: Parameter α1: How Many Real Zeros?
tasks.context:
Let $g_k(x)=x^3-kx$ with real $k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

(Exam variant 90.)
statements: If $k>0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k=0$, then $g_k$ has three distinct real zeros.
If $k<0$, then $g_k$ has only one real zero.
The leading coefficient of $g_k$ depends on $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For a positive parameter the quadratic factor $x^{2}-k$ has two real roots, distinct from each other and from $0$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(x)=x(x^{2}-k)$$

With $k=9$ those roots are $\pm 3$, so the zero set is $\{-3,0,3\}$.

$$g_{9}(3)=27-27$$

$$27-27$$

$$g_{9}(3)=0$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

Three different real numbers, and the same counting $0,\pm\sqrt{k}$ works for every $k>0$. Three distinct real zeros occur.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The zero-parameter member of the family is a monomial cube, whose only real root is the origin.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x^{3}$$

$$g_{0}(x)=x\cdot x\cdot x$$

Distinct zeros ignore multiplicity: a squared factor still counts as one abscissa.

That is a single distinct zero of multiplicity three, not three different axis crossings. For instance $g_{0}(1)=1\neq 0$ and $g_{0}(-1)=-1\neq 0$. Distinctness fails as soon as $k=0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

When $k$ is negative the quadratic $x^{2}-k$ never hits zero, because it equals $x^{2}$ plus a positive constant.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{-1}(x)=x^{3}+x$$

$$x^{3}+x=x(x^{2}+1)$$

$$x^{2}+1\ge 1>0$$

The only real solution of $x(x^{2}+1)=0$ is $x=0$. A second sample $k=-4$ gives $x(x^{2}+4)$, again only $x=0$. Every negative $k$ leaves this same single real zero.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Write two members side by side and compare the coefficients of $x^{3}$.

$$g_{2}(x)=x^{3}-2x$$

$$g_{7}(x)=x^{3}-7x$$

Read the highest written power whose coefficient is nonzero.

A nonzero coefficient of that highest power is what makes the degree exact.

Both are monic cubics: the number in front of $x^{3}$ is $1$ in each case. Changing $k$ only changes the coefficient of $x$, from $-2$ to $-7$ in the sample. The leading coefficient does not depend on $k$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Every power in $x^{3}-kx$ is odd, so replacing $x$ by $-x$ multiplies the whole formula by $-1$.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g_{k}(-x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

$$-g_{k}(x)=-x^{3}+kx$$

Equivalently, every surviving power in the expansion must be odd.

The two sides match for every real $k$. In particular

$$g_{0}(-x)=-x^{3}$$

$$g_{0}(-x)=-g_{0}(x)$$

 still holds, and

$$g_{1}(-2)=-8+2$$

$$g_{1}(-2)=-6$$

$$g_{1}(-2)=-g_{1}(2)$$

. The family is odd for every real $k$.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The family is given explicitly, with the parameter sitting on a lower term, so the leading term never sees it.

$$g_k(x)=x^3-kx$$

$$g(x)=x \left(- k + x^{2}\right)$$

Factor $x(x^{2}-k)$ to read the root count from the sign of $k$.

Degree and the leading coefficient are read from the highest written power whose coefficient is not zero.

Parity is a coefficient reading: only odd powers make an odd map, only even powers make an even map.

$$-(x^{3}-kx)=-g_{k}(x)$$

$$g_{2}(-1)=1$$

$$-g_{2}(1)=-(1-2)$$

$$-g_{2}(1)=1$$

. Each $g_{k}$ is an odd function.
